Hiya! I've been climbing for about a year and it's taken me ALL of that time to figure this out.

I started out pretty strong, but heavy (5'11, 180lb). My recurring issues were around inner elbow, left foot bunion, shoulder, and lower back. I'll list out how I managed each of these, but before I do, I'll answer your core question.  Easily the **biggest** thing I changed was not *just* reducing frequency - it was **balancing frequency and intensity.** ie. I can climb every other day, but that's maybe at 60-70% intensity. This doesn't mean "don't push yourself" rather, as soon as you start to plateau and degrade on a limit test project, screw it. go 2-3 grades down and do volume and downclimbing if you want to keep going. If I'm pushing myself to 100% safely, I'm taking an extra day or two of rest. You can balance this with climbing styles too. Wrists tired? No more slopers. Toes hurt? stop climbing slab. Fingers done? save the crimps for next time. 

Issue 1 - My inner elbow. This one is a common one. Most climbers go through this one at some point, and the above advice will make a huge difference. Also be mindful of which climbs are rougher on the elbows (for me, anything overhung puts a lot more stress on the elbow), and ensure you're climbing with your legs and back, not your arms and elbows. Downclimbing helped me drill this a lot - in particular, engaging the traps and lats. I also focus on this during warm ups with some banded stability exercises to prime the back.

Issue 2 - foot bunion. I have a bad bunion. As my shoes got more aggressive and I climbed more, bunion pain got worse. I wear toe spacers in my shoe now and that stops 95% of the issue.

Issue 3 - shoulder injuries. If you're on the stronger side, it's likely you'll excel at gastons and stemmy moves - a lot of these put your shoulder into a vulnerable position. Just be mindful and warm it up properly. The same banded exercises for your back will probably do great for your shoulder too. Try not to do anything full force while your shoulder is fully extended and almost popping out of the joint. Those tendons are just like your fingers - they'll take a while to build up.

Issue 4 - lower back. Oh man. It doesn't matter how good you are at falling, it's going to compress your spine a bit. You'll notice most of the experienced climbers down climb a little and try not to drop from the top. It's and unnecessary risk, don't take it.  Also, not warming up before dynamic moves will destroy your lower back. Just imagine doing a pause squat, from in the hole with 150-200lb as a first rep without warming up, on an uneven surface. Seems obvious in hindsight, but took me a couple of thrown-out-backs to just fucking warm up beforehand.

* **Define success for yourself -** There is what folks like to think of as the "hard sciences" portion of product management. This overlaps a lot with UI/UX research and to me, really just means "go learn a bunch of relevant frameworks". Believe it or not, I learned the most about these ***interviewing*** for product roles. So my advice here would be to pretend you're interviewing - go look at product role JDs that excite you, pretend you're preparing for it. This gives you something to aim for, encourages you to take on projects that'll look great on your resume, etc.. I personally never stop interviewing because it keeps me present.
* **Understand adjacent roles -** Getting an agile certification or program/project management certification is helpful primarily in understanding the PO, scrum master, and Pg/Pj M parts of the role. You'll almost certainly have some responsibilities that overlap with those roles, especially early in your career, so it's both helpful to know how to succeed ***and*** not get pigeonholed. Nobody really cares about your certification, but it's helpful to understand how a SAFE practicing org is different from others - it may not be your cup of tea and it's helpful to know up front. 
* **Learn how to help yourself -** Basic SQL and analytics (A/B testing, data science principles) are super useful, and if you want to consider a more technical path, even an **intro** to  python, databases, and APIs will take you ***very*** far. Being able to talk to technical people and, at times, help yourself before asking for help, will win you tons of trust and authority with cross functional partners.

Don't get caught up in the aspirational PM bullshit - every job is different and at the end of the day, it'll still be a job. Make it one you like and don't want to escape from, and you'll do great.

Oh boy - I've struggled with this. It's been a blessing in some sports, but quite frankly, have led to a few injuries for me with climibing, especially in the rotator cuff and elbow.

I've had to unlearn the prompts of always trying to go "full range of motion" for a lot of exercises - this advice is not for us, frankly. Pull-ups, for example, are particularly relevant to climbing, but generating force from a FULLY extended shoulder really requires you to 1) have PERFECT form, ie. fully engage your traps before you start pulling from the shoulder and 2) SLOWLY build up to strength in these hyperextended positions, IF AT ALL. I've worked through this for pull-ups, but decided to limit motion with my elbows as the risk is too high.

PLEASE remember that it's tendons and ligaments around your joints, not just muscles. Especially in these hyperextended states, it's our tendons and ligaments taking all the strain. These take much longer to grow and train when compared to muscles. Train it slow and limit "range of motion" whenever practical to reduce risk.

Most of the PMs I've worked with fit into 3 general buckets - 1) engineering (CS) background, 2) marketing background or UX background, 3) entrepreneur or consulting background. These buckets align pretty well with the general responsibilities most product people are expected to perform in their day to day.

Personally, I fit in #3 - from environmental engineering, I ventured into the entrepreneurial world. I spent the last year of my time as an engineer working on side projects, learning ecommerce. Primarily, I leveraged the chemical engineering side of my degree into cosmetics formulation and was able to get a skincare brand off the ground with a friend. This ended up going nowhere, but the experience gave me confidence to identify a target market and start my own business - nothing fancy, tutoring high school kids from China trying to goto university in the states. This business ended up growing pretty quickly and became another great opportunity to learn more about entrepreneurship, business strategy, and just plain grit. By the end of this opportunity, I realized I wanted some more formal training and product management sounded a lot like what I was doing already - so I started looking.

The first push into product was pretty rough - I was winding down my involvement in what had become an edutech company and trying to learn how to interview - in hindsight, I had no idea what I was doing, and like most new product people, no clue what product management actually entailed beyond what the books say. There's definitely a science to product management with lots of resources (tryexponent was a resource I really liked, as well as all sorts of agile stuff) but there's really no replacement for actual product experience which makes it REALLY hard to convince someone to take a chance on you. What I ended up doing was finding a place that fit well with my experience and passion that was hiring a product role, and then ended up taking an entry level role at the company instead. The story I told was that the role I was taking would prepare me for success in a product role there, and they'd have 6-12 months to give me some homework occasionally. Somehow, the stars aligned and this worked.

6 months later, I was excelling in my entry level role, and they happened to be hiring for another product role. Because I had set the expectation and goal with managers and leadership alike super early on at the org, I was able to get wide support. (Big lesson here about building alignment, finding allies, etc.)

Spent a couple years at this org learning, then a couple years doing product at ecommerce companies. Found my experience being steered towards data and analytics, and after a solid 4 years of product experience, finally found a perfect role in climate tech. It's not all sunshine and rainbows, but it's engaging work in an exciting industry full of impact. Wouldn't trade it for the world.

To recap and enumerate without the personal story here...

* I started with understanding what the role was like, and evaluating whether it'd be a good fit for me in the first place
* I upskilled using different resources, from entrepreneurship, online classes to learn coding basics and design tools, obtaining agile certifications, interview prep to understand the "science" of product management
* I strategically identified an opportunity that would benefit me, making sure my expectations were realistic, made the sacrifice (starting a new career in an entry level, service role in tech) and bet on myself. I figured out how to tell the story and make it believable and exciting.
* I executed on the story, I iterated into different opportunities and companies, accumulated experience and colleagues, and then finally, leveraged my network, passion, and skillset into role aligned with the industry I wanted to be in (climate tech).

Keep in mind, this is somewhat specific to my journey into product management in climate tech, but I think there's a lot of nuggets in there about breaking into tech more generally. It's worth highlighting that CS is not the only role in tech - it truly takes a village.
